claims.text: The starting FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles are solid and compositionally homogeneous, with minimal pre-existing phase separation.
Premelting and melting in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles are primarily governed by thermally activated surface and grain-boundary diffusion.
Thermally activated diffusion promotes elemental segregation at nanoparticle surfaces and grain boundaries.
Cu preferentially migrates to FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticle surfaces and grain boundaries as the melting regime is approached.
Residual impurity atoms preferentially migrate to surfaces and grain boundaries during heating.
Cu is the low-melting-point component responsible for especially important segregation effects in this alloy.
Cu and impurity enrichment lowers the local melting point at surfaces and grain boundaries.
The locally reduced melting point initiates a thin liquid-like interfacial layer before bulk melting.
The interfacial liquid layer provides a pathway for progression from premelting to complete melting.
At otherwise fixed particle size, composition, atmosphere, and heating rate, impurity-enriched nanoparticles will form a liquid layer at a lower temperature than high-purity nanoparticles.
Enhanced surface segregation will correlate with an earlier premelting onset.
Early premelting will produce a DSC endotherm and TEM-visible liquid-like surface features.
Complete melting will proceed through growth and coalescence of initially localized liquid regions.
Nanoparticle size, shape, and defect distribution may modulate premelting onset kinetics.
Holding nanoparticle size distribution, heating rate, atmosphere, and bulk alloy composition constant provides a controlled comparison of impurity effects.

The mechanism would be falsified if no Cu or impurity segregation precedes melting, or if impurity-enriched and high-purity samples show similar melting onset and morphology without a premelting liquid layer.
